meta.title: Getting a Powerful Person to Take You On
meta.subtitle: How patronage actually gets bought, kept, and survived
meta.description: A closed file on the oldest career move there is: finding someone with real power, making yourself worth their time, asking once and asking right, and staying attached to their name until you have one of your own. Twenty-two moves, in the order you will need them.
meta.author: AI

categories.label: Be Useful Before You Are Known

cards.title: Pick Someone Who Needs a Bench, Not a Fan
cards.principle: Greene: Law 19 — Know Who You Are Dealing With
cards.remember: Back the person who is short on people, not short on praise.
cards.when: You are choosing which senior person to spend the next two years getting close to.
cards.hook: Powerful people have enough admirers. Very few have enough hands.
cards.truth:
Patronage is a trade, not a gift. They take you on because they are short of something.
• Find the one who is building something and lacks people.
• They will spend real credit on you, because they need the seat filled.
• A person with a full bench only wants applause. You will get nothing back.
cards.theySee: A junior person who turns up where the work is piling up and nobody else volunteers.

signals.t: They just got a bigger job or a new team to build
They complain that they cannot find good people
Their project slipped a deadline in the last quarter
The same two names do everything for them
Someone senior left their team in the last six months

steps.title: List five names
steps.desc: Write the five people above you with real power over budget or hiring.

steps.title: Mark who is growing
steps.desc: Next to each name, write what they got in the last year: a team, a budget, a mandate, nothing.

steps.title: Pick the one with a gap
steps.desc: Choose the person with the biggest new job and the fewest people. Drop the rest.

cards.script: "I hear you picked up the platform group on top of your own. What is the thing that is not getting done because nobody has time?"
cards.example: Dev had two options: a famous VP with a packed team, and a director who had just absorbed a second org. He picked the director. Within four months he ran her weekly ops review, because nobody else was free to.
cards.watchFor: They answer your question with a real problem instead of a polite line.
cards.ifItFails: They give you a smooth non-answer and change the subject — that means their bench is full or you are not on their radar yet. Do not ask twice. Go to the person one level below them who owns the mess, and get known there first. Say: "Who actually runs that day to day? I would like to help on it."
cards.counter:
If someone senior suddenly wants a mentor in you, they want your access, not your wisdom.
• Notice what they ask about: your network, not your judgment.
• Say: "Happy to help. What are you trying to get to?"
• Give advice freely. Give introductions slowly and one at a time.
cards.insight: Everyone chases the biggest name because the name is easy to see. The gap is that the biggest name needs you least. Do not do this to someone who signs your reviews and already has a favorite — you will just look like a third wheel. The next question is whether their new mandate survives a year.

cards.title: Check Whether Their Last Protege Rose or Vanished
cards.remember: Look at who they helped before. That is your forecast.
cards.when: You are about to attach yourself to a senior person and you only know their reputation.
cards.hook: Their last three proteges already ran this experiment for you. Go read the results.
cards.truth:
People are consistent with proteges. The pattern repeats on you.
• Find the names they backed two and five years ago.
• Some patrons promote people out. Some burn them and keep the credit.
• Nobody checks this, because it feels rude to ask. Ask anyway.
cards.theySee: Nothing. This move happens away from them, in other people's calendars.

signals.t: Their old team members now hold bigger jobs elsewhere
Two people left their team and nobody talks about where they went
They say "I built that" about work a team did
Former reports still reply to their messages within a day

steps.title: Pull the list
steps.desc: Find three people who worked directly for them two or more years ago.

steps.title: Ask one of them for coffee
steps.desc: Pick the one who left, not the one who stayed. Leavers tell the truth.

steps.title: Ask the one question
steps.desc: Ask what happened to their career in the two years after they worked for that person.

cards.script: "I am thinking about moving under Ray. You worked for him. Did working for him make your next job easier or harder?"
cards.example: Priya nearly joined a famous managing director. She called two of his old analysts first. Both said the same thing: he took every deal credit and neither got a sponsor for promotion. She joined a quieter partner and made VP in three years.
cards.watchFor: They pause before answering, then choose their words carefully.
cards.ifItFails: The alumni all give you clean, careful praise — that itself is data, because scared people sound identical. Ask a second question that is hard to answer smoothly: "Who did he push for promotion last cycle?" If nobody can name a person, you have your answer.
cards.counter:
If someone runs this check on you, they will ask your old reports about you.
• Notice a junior person asking your team about your history.
• Say nothing about it. Fix the record instead.
• Push one person's promotion this cycle and make it public.
cards.insight: Most people research the company and never research the person who will own their next two years. The trap is that a charming patron and a generous one look identical in a first meeting. The only difference is on other people's resumes.

cards.title: Pick the Person Rising, Not the Person at the Top
cards.principle: Machiavelli: The Prince — Fortune Favors the Rising House
cards.remember: Attach to someone climbing. Their rise carries you up.
cards.when: You can get access to a mid-level person who is climbing fast, or the edge of a famous executive's circle.
cards.hook: At the top, you are one of forty. On the way up, you are one of three. Only one of those gets you a seat.
cards.truth:
You do not ride someone's power. You ride the change in their power.
• Join before the rise. The seat is cheap then.
• When they move up, they take the people who were there early.
• People at the peak have nowhere to take you. They are defending, not building.
cards.theySee: An early believer who showed up before the promotion, not after it.

signals.t: Their unit grew two quarters in a row
Leadership now asks them to present at the all-hands
The CEO's office calls them directly
They opened three new roles this quarter

steps.title: Find the climbers
steps.desc: Name two people who got more responsibility in the last six months.

steps.title: Get one meeting
steps.desc: Ask for 20 minutes about their new area. Not about your career.

steps.title: Say you want in early
steps.desc: Tell them plainly you want to work on what they are building next.

cards.script: "You are going to need more people for this in about two quarters. I want to be one of them. What should I be good at by then?"
cards.example: Omar skipped the famous CTO and latched onto a director running a new billing team. Eighteen months later she ran engineering for the region. She took four people with her. Omar was one of them.
cards.watchFor: They start telling you about a role that does not exist yet.
cards.ifItFails: They say they have no headroom and no budget. Do not wait quietly — that is how you get forgotten. Get on one of their projects part-time from your current job and make it visible. Send: "I have four hours a week. Give me the piece nobody has picked up."
cards.counter:
If a junior person attaches to you early, they are buying an option on your rise.
• Notice who helps you before you have anything to give.
• Say: "You are early. I will remember it."
• Keep the list short and actually honor it. Broken promises here spread fast.
cards.insight: Everyone wants the meeting with the most powerful person in the building. That meeting is worth almost nothing, because that person's calendar is already spoken for. The harder part is judging who is really rising versus who is just loud this quarter.

cards.title: Go Where They Already Are Instead of Asking for Time
cards.remember: Be in the room five times before you ask for anything.
cards.when: You want a senior person's attention and you have no reason to be on their calendar.
cards.hook: A cold meeting request costs them 30 minutes. Standing in the same room costs them nothing.
cards.truth:
Familiar faces get trust that new faces have to earn.
• Find the recurring thing they attend and attend it too.
• After a few times, their brain files you as "one of us".
• Most people skip this and open with a cold ask. That ask reads as a demand.
cards.theySee: A familiar face who keeps turning up at the same meetings and events they do.

signals.t: They attend the same review or forum every month
They get coffee at the same time each morning
They speak at internal sessions anyone can join
They nod at you in the hallway without knowing your name

steps.title: Find the recurring room
steps.desc: Check their public calendar or ask around for one meeting they never miss.

steps.title: Get in it
steps.desc: Ask the meeting owner if you can join as a listener. Most say yes.

steps.title: Say one useful thing on visit three
steps.desc: Stay silent the first two times. On the third, add one short fact nobody else has.

cards.script: (To the meeting owner) "Can I sit in on the Thursday ops review as a listener? I keep touching this work from the edge and I would rather hear it directly."
cards.example: Nina could not get 15 minutes with the COO. She joined his Thursday metrics review as a silent observer for six weeks. On week seven she corrected a number nobody else caught. He asked for her name and emailed her Monday.
cards.watchFor: They greet you before you greet them.
cards.ifItFails: You get blocked from the room, or you attend and stay invisible. Switch from the meeting to its output — read the notes and send one correction to the owner each week. Say: "Slide 6 uses last quarter's churn. Here is the current one." Now the room hears your name without you in it.
cards.counter:
If someone keeps appearing at your edges, they are building familiarity before an ask.
• Notice a new face at three of your recurring meetings.
• Say: "You keep turning up. What are you after?"
• Naming it early costs you nothing and puts you in control of the timing.
cards.insight: Access is mostly a seating problem, not a persuasion problem. The trap is staying a face and never becoming a name — the room grants comfort but not credit. The move that follows is making them say your name out loud.

cards.title: Win Over Their Assistant First
cards.principle: Gracián: Know Who Guards the Door
cards.remember: The assistant decides who gets time. Treat them like the decision maker.
cards.when: You need time with someone whose calendar is managed by another person.
cards.hook: You are not negotiating with the boss. You are negotiating with the person who owns the calendar.
cards.truth:
The gatekeeper is not an obstacle. They are a judge with real power.
• They sort every request into urgent, later, or never.
• Be easy for them: short ask, clear reason, flexible time.
• Almost everyone is rude or slippery with them. Being decent is a real edge.
cards.theySee: A person who makes their job easier instead of harder, and who remembers their name.

signals.t: Your emails to the boss get answered by the assistant
They say the boss is slammed for the next three weeks
A slot opens for someone else on the day you were refused
They greet you by name without checking a list

steps.title: Learn their name and use it
steps.desc: Get the assistant's name right and say it in every message.

steps.title: Make the ask tiny
steps.desc: Ask for 15 minutes, not 30, and offer three windows.

steps.title: Tell them the point in one line
steps.desc: Give them a single sentence they can paste into the invite.

cards.script: "Hi Carla — 15 minutes with Ray, any time that suits his week. One topic: the vendor renewal that hits in November. Feel free to move it if something bigger lands."
cards.example: Tom's meeting requests died for four months. He then sent Carla a one-line purpose and three flexible windows, and thanked her by name. She put him in a cancelled slot the next week. He has been on the calendar quarterly since.
cards.watchFor: The assistant offers you a slot you did not ask for.
cards.ifItFails: They keep saying there is no time. Stop asking for a meeting and ask for a decision instead: send a half-page with two options and a date. Say: "No meeting needed. If he picks A or B by Friday, I will run with it." A request that removes work gets through where a request that adds work does not.
cards.counter:
If someone is unusually warm to your assistant, they are working the door.
• Notice compliments aimed at your gatekeeper, not at you.
• Ask your assistant: "What did they actually want?"
• Assistants read intent better than you do. Trust their read.
cards.insight: Most people treat the calendar as a queue and it is not — it is a judgment. The tradeoff is that once the assistant vouches for you, you cannot waste the slot. The next question is what you say in the first eight minutes.

cards.title: Get Introduced Instead of Introducing Yourself
cards.remember: Someone they trust should say your name first.
cards.when: You have one shot at a powerful person and no existing relationship with them.
cards.hook: A stranger's pitch gets 30 seconds of patience. A friend's recommendation gets 30 minutes.
cards.truth:
Trust moves through people, not through credentials.
• Find the person who has both their ear and your respect.
• Ask that person for a sentence, not a favor.
• Write the sentence yourself. Busy people forward what is already written.
cards.theySee: A person their trusted colleague personally vouched for, in that colleague's own words.

signals.t: You and they both work closely with the same third person
They publicly thanked someone you already know well
Your contact forwards mail to them and gets a same-day reply
You did real work for your contact in the last year

steps.title: Name the bridge
steps.desc: Write down who knows both of you and owes you nothing bad.

steps.title: Write the intro for them
steps.desc: Send your contact two sentences they can forward without editing.

steps.title: Give them an easy out
steps.desc: Say it is fine to skip it. People say yes more when refusing is free.

cards.script: "Would you forward this to Ray if you think it holds up? 'Tom fixed our renewal mess last quarter. He has one idea about your November contract. Worth 15 minutes.' Totally fine to pass."
cards.example: Leah wanted a hedge fund partner's attention. She did not email him. She asked a former colleague to send one line: "Leah found the error in our model before the auditors did." The partner replied within two hours.
cards.watchFor: The powerful person opens with your introducer's name, not with a question about who you are.
cards.ifItFails: Your bridge goes quiet or sends a limp version. Do not chase them twice — that burns the contact. Go to a second bridge with a smaller, more specific ask, or write directly and name the shared person up front: "Sara Ng suggested I flag this to you directly." Do not use a name that will not back you if checked.
cards.counter:
If someone arrives wrapped in a trusted name, the name is doing the selling.
• Notice that you feel warm before they have said anything.
• Ask the introducer privately: "How well do you actually know them?"
• Judge the work in the first meeting, not the referral.
cards.insight: Credentials travel badly; vouching travels well. The trap is spending a strong bridge on a weak ask — you only get one clean introduction per contact per year. The harder part is being worth the vouch when you walk in.

cards.title: Solve the Problem They Complain About in Public
cards.remember: Listen for their complaint. Fix it before they ask.
cards.when: A powerful person says out loud, in a meeting or a post, that something is broken.
cards.hook: They just told a room what is hurting them. Most people nodded. You go fix it.
cards.truth:
An unasked-for fix creates a debt that an asked-for favor never does.
• Powerful people repeat their real problems in public constantly.
• Bring the fix, not the offer to help. Offers create work.
• The debt is strongest before you ask for anything. Do not cash it the same week.
cards.theySee: A person who hands them a finished answer to the thing they were complaining about on Tuesday.

signals.t: They mentioned the same problem in two different meetings
Their tone changed when the topic came up
Nobody in the room volunteered to take it
The problem has a deadline attached to it

steps.title: Write the complaint down
steps.desc: Capture their exact words the next time they say a thing is broken.

steps.title: Build the smallest real fix
steps.desc: Spend one weekend, not one quarter. A working half beats a proposed whole.

steps.title: Send it with no ask attached
steps.desc: One paragraph, the artifact, and nothing else. No meeting request.

cards.script: "You said the regional numbers take three days to pull. Here is a sheet that pulls them in ten minutes. It is yours, no strings."
cards.example: Ben heard the CFO complain twice that board slides took a week. He rebuilt the data pull over a weekend and emailed it with one line and no ask. Two months later the CFO put him on the board prep team.
cards.watchFor: They forward your work to someone else with your name on it.
cards.ifItFails: They ignore it or thank you with one word. Do not resend. Wait for the problem to bite again, then reply into that moment: "This is the thing from last month. It is still running if you want it." A fix offered at the moment of pain lands where the same fix offered early did not.
cards.counter:
If someone hands you unasked-for work, they are opening an account you will be asked to pay.
• Notice a gift that arrives with no request attached.
• Say: "This is good. What are you working on that I can look at?"
• Pay it back small and early, before the big ask arrives.
cards.insight: Help offered is a cost to them; help delivered is a gift. The trap is delivering something they did not want and calling it a gift — then you are the person who created a review task. The move that follows is doing it twice before you speak.

cards.title: Send Them Work, Never Requests
cards.remember: Every message you send should give them something.
cards.when: You want to stay on a powerful person's radar for months without a formal role.
cards.hook: Ten messages that give. Then one that asks. That ratio is the whole game.
cards.truth:
Your name gets filed under what your messages cost them.
• Each note should shorten their day, not lengthen it.
• Send facts, numbers, and finished pieces. Never send "thoughts".
• Most people check in to stay visible. A check-in is a small tax.
cards.theySee: A person whose emails they open first, because those emails contain something useful.

signals.t: They reply to your notes within a day
They pass your material to their team
They start asking you for things unprompted
Your last three notes got no reply

steps.title: Make a give list
steps.desc: Write three things you can send them: a number, a contact, a competitor fact.

steps.title: Send one this week
steps.desc: Three sentences maximum, no meeting request, no signature block essay.

steps.title: Log the date
steps.desc: Keep a note of what you sent and when. Do not repeat yourself.

cards.script: "Two things you may not have: Acme cut their price 12% in the Midwest, and their VP of Sales left Friday. No reply needed."
cards.example: Kofi sent a partner one short market note a month for a year and never asked for anything. In month thirteen the partner called him about a job before it was posted. Kofi had never applied.
cards.watchFor: They reply with a question instead of a thank you.
cards.ifItFails: Three notes get no reply. Change the type of give, not the frequency. Stop sending information and send a person instead — introduce them to someone they want to meet. Say: "You mentioned wanting to meet someone at Acme. Dana runs their pricing. Want the intro?"
cards.counter:
If someone only ever gives, they are saving up for one large ask.
• Notice a pattern of gifts with no request for months.
• Say: "You have sent a lot my way. What do you need?"
• Settle the account on your terms before they set the price.
cards.insight: Attention is rented monthly and paid in usefulness. The tradeoff is that giving with no ask for too long makes you furniture. The next question is when to convert, and that timing is the whole next chapter.

cards.title: Become the First Person Who Tells Them Bad News
cards.remember: Bring bad news fast. That is how you become trusted.
cards.when: You learn something that will hurt a powerful person before they hear it from anyone else.
cards.hook: Everyone brings them good news. The person who brings the bad news early becomes necessary.
cards.truth:
Powerful people are surrounded by filters. They know it and it frightens them.
• Deliver the bad fact plainly, early, and without drama.
• You become the one channel they believe.
• The trap is becoming only bad news. Always bring the fix in the same breath.
cards.theySee: A person who tells them the ugly thing on Monday instead of letting them find it on Friday.

signals.t: Their reports say everything is on track when it is not
They learned about a problem from someone outside the company
Issues reach them only after they became expensive
They start calling you to check what they were told

steps.title: Confirm the fact
steps.desc: Check it twice. One wrong alarm ends this move permanently.

steps.title: Lead with the fact
steps.desc: First sentence is the bad news. No build-up, no cushion.

steps.title: Attach one option
steps.desc: Give them one thing they can decide today, not a list of five.

cards.script: "The Denver contract will miss the renewal date. It is not recoverable this week. One option: we extend 30 days at current terms. I can have that letter out today if you want it."
cards.example: Ana learned a launch would slip nine days. Her peers waited for the next review. She told the SVP that afternoon with a revised date and a customer note already drafted. He started calling her directly before every board meeting.
cards.watchFor: They stop what they are doing and ask you a follow-up question.
cards.ifItFails: They shoot the messenger and get cold. Do not retreat into silence — that proves the filter works. Put the next one in writing, short and factual, and copy nobody: "Flagging early so it is on the record: the date moves. Here is the fix." Do not run this move on a boss who punishes people publicly for problems they did not create.
cards.counter:
If someone always brings you bad news first, check whether they also create it.
• Notice a person who is present at every fire.
• Ask: "When did you first know about this?"
• Reward the early warning. Watch the timeline for the pattern.
cards.insight: Filtered leaders pay a premium for one honest channel. The trap is that the channel only stays valuable while it is rare — three people doing this and you are just the pessimist. The harder part is bringing bad news without owning it.

cards.title: Take the Job Nobody Else Wants
cards.principle: Greene: Law 7 — Get Others to Do the Work, Inverted
cards.remember: Grab the ugly job. It comes with the boss attached.
cards.when: A senior person needs someone to run something thankless, messy, or boring.
cards.hook: The glamour jobs have twelve applicants. The ugly one has none, and it comes with their phone number.
cards.truth:
Ugly work is the cheapest access money can buy.
• Nobody competes for it, so you get it immediately.
• Ugly work needs decisions, and decisions need them. You get their time weekly.
• The trap is staying there. Take it, fix it, hand it off in a year.
cards.theySee: A person who put their hand up for the thing the room went quiet about.

signals.t: Nobody volunteers when they name the task
The work is fixing someone else's mess
The task needs a decision from them every week
The task has been unassigned for over a month

steps.title: Spot the silence
steps.desc: Watch for the item that gets skipped in every status meeting.

steps.title: Claim it out loud
steps.desc: Say you will take it, in the meeting, in front of everyone.

steps.title: Set a weekly ten minutes
steps.desc: Tell them you need ten minutes each week to unblock it. That is the real prize.

cards.script: "I will take the audit remediation. I need ten minutes with you every Tuesday to clear blockers. That is all."
cards.example: Raj volunteered for the compliance backlog nobody touched for two years. It bought him a standing Tuesday slot with the general counsel. When a policy director role opened, the GC did not post it.
cards.watchFor: They give you a standing slot on their calendar.
cards.ifItFails: You get the ugly job and no access — they hand it off and disappear. Force the contact by making the decisions theirs: send a weekly three-line note with one question that only they can answer. "Two done, one blocked. I need your call on the vendor by Thursday or it slips."
cards.counter:
If someone hands you thankless work with warm words, check what access comes with it.
• Notice praise that arrives instead of resources.
• Say: "I will take it if I get a weekly slot with you."
• No access, no deal. Ugly work without contact is just ugly work.
cards.insight: The cost of entry is low exactly where the prestige is low. The trap is that ugly work is sticky — the person who fixed it gets it forever. The move that follows is naming your successor before you are asked.

cards.title: Make Your First Ask Small and Exact
cards.remember: Ask for one small thing they can do in five minutes.
cards.when: You have been useful for months and you are ready to ask a powerful person for something.
cards.hook: A big first ask asks them to bet on you. A small one just asks them to say yes.
cards.truth:
The first yes matters more than the size of what you get.
• Ask for something specific that costs them under ten minutes.
• Once they help you, their brain files you as someone they help.
• Most people wait and then ask for a job. That is the last ask, not the first.
cards.theySee: A person who asked for one clear, small thing instead of a vague favor.

signals.t: You have sent them useful things three or more times
They message you without you starting it
You can name exactly what you want in one sentence
Your ask takes them under ten minutes

steps.title: Write the ask in one line
steps.desc: If it takes two sentences to explain, it is too big for the first one.

steps.title: Name the cost to them
steps.desc: Say how long it will take. "Five minutes" removes their main objection.

steps.title: Send it alone
steps.desc: Do not bundle the ask with a give. That makes the give look like payment.

cards.script: "One small ask: would you forward my note to Dana at Acme with a line saying we worked together? Five minutes, and I will take it from there."
cards.example: Sam spent eight months sending a director useful market notes. His first ask was one forwarded email. She sent it in four minutes. Three months later he asked her to back him for a promotion and she said yes without pausing.
cards.watchFor: They do it the same day and tell you it is done.
cards.ifItFails: They agree and then forget. Do not nudge with a guilt line. Make it trivially easy and give them a deadline: "Rewrote it so you can just hit forward. If Thursday does not work, I will go another route — no problem either way." Giving them an exit makes the yes cheaper.
cards.counter:
If someone asks for something tiny after months of gifts, the small ask is a test.
• Notice a request that is oddly easy to grant.
• Say yes if you mean it, no if you do not. Do not stall.
• A vague yes now becomes a bigger ask in six weeks.
cards.insight: The first yes changes how they see themselves in relation to you. The tradeoff is you spend the account on something small. The next question is how fast you can come back for the real thing without looking like a meter running.

cards.title: Ask for Advice, Not for a Job
cards.principle: Flynn and Lake: Advice Seeking Raises Status
cards.remember: Ask how they would do it. Do not ask them to do it.
cards.when: You want a powerful person's backing but a direct request would be too big to grant.
cards.hook: Ask for a job and you become a problem to solve. Ask for advice and you become their project.
cards.truth:
Advice makes them a stakeholder without costing them anything.
• People who advise you feel responsible for how it turns out.
• Their brain rates you smarter for asking, not weaker.
• The trap is asking for advice and then ignoring it. That ends the relationship.
cards.theySee: A person who wants their judgment, not their favors, and who takes notes.

signals.t: They talk longer when asked how they did something
They watch to see whether you write anything down
They ask what happened with their suggestion
They deflect when people ask them for introductions

steps.title: Pick one real decision
steps.desc: Choose something you are actually deciding this month, not a hypothetical.

steps.title: Ask how they would decide it
steps.desc: Use their experience, not their power: "How did you handle this at your level?"

steps.title: Report back in two weeks
steps.desc: Tell them what you did and what happened. This step is the whole move.

cards.script: "I am deciding between the platform role and staying in my group. You made that exact call in 2019. How did you think about it?"
cards.example: Grace never asked the SVP for a role. She asked how he chose between two paths early in his career and then told him what she did with his answer. Six weeks later he called her about an opening and said it was his idea.
cards.watchFor: They ask you what happened with their advice before you tell them.
cards.ifItFails: They give you a two-line brush-off. Narrow it until it is flattering to answer: ask about a specific decision they are known for. "When you shut down the Atlanta site, what made you pull the trigger that quarter?" Specific questions about their own wins get answered when general ones do not.
cards.counter:
If someone keeps asking your advice, they are making you invested in them.
• Notice questions about your past decisions, not your resources.
• Say: "Here is how I would do it. What will you actually do?"
• Give advice once. Watch whether they act before you give more.
cards.insight: Asking for help lowers your status; asking for judgment raises it. The trap is that advice creates an obligation on you — they will check. The move that follows is showing up with the result before they ask.

cards.title: Give Them a Date So They Can Say No Fast
cards.remember: Put a date on the ask. A slow no is the expensive one.
cards.when: You have made a real ask and the powerful person has gone quiet for two weeks.
cards.hook: Silence is not thinking. Silence is your request sitting in a pile below everything urgent.
cards.truth:
A request with no date never competes with a request that has one.
• Attach a real event, not an invented one. They can smell a fake clock.
• Give them a clean way to decline. That is what makes them answer.
• Most people chase with reminders. Reminders teach them you will wait.
cards.theySee: A person who respects their time enough to make refusing easy.

signals.t: They have not replied in two weeks
They said "let me think about it" twice
Something in your life actually expires on a date
You have a second path you can genuinely take

steps.title: Find the real date
steps.desc: Name the thing that actually expires: an offer, a hiring cycle, a budget close.

steps.title: Send one line with the date
steps.desc: State the date, the ask, and the alternative you will take without them.

steps.title: Take the other path if the date passes
steps.desc: Do not extend it. Extending once ends every deadline you ever set.

cards.script: "I need to answer the other team by the 30th. If you want me on your group, I need a yes before then. If not, no hard feelings — I will take the other one."
cards.example: Marcus waited five weeks for a director to confirm a transfer. He sent one line naming a real competing offer and a Friday date. The director approved it Wednesday. Marcus had the other offer in writing first.
cards.watchFor: They reply within 48 hours after two weeks of nothing.
cards.ifItFails: They call the deadline and let it pass. You must take the other path — bluffing here destroys you. Go, and send one clean note that keeps the door open: "I took the other role. Still want to stay in touch." Do not use this on someone who controls your only option; without a real alternative it is not a deadline, it is a tantrum.
cards.counter:
If someone hands you a deadline, check whether the clock is real.
• Notice a date with no named event behind it.
• Ask: "What happens on the 30th specifically?"
• If they cannot name it, treat the date as theater and take your time.
cards.insight: Deadlines only work if you are willing to lose. The tradeoff is that every deadline spends goodwill, whichever way it goes. The next question is whether you can afford the answer you might get.

cards.title: Let Them Introduce You in the Room
cards.remember: When they say your name, the room re-rates you.
cards.when: You are in a meeting or event where your patron knows everyone and you know nobody.
cards.hook: You can spend two years earning a room's respect. Or they can hand it to you in nine words.
cards.truth:
A room's opinion of you is set by who vouches for you, not by what you do there.
• Give them the line you want them to use, before the event.
• They will say a version of it, and the room will repeat it.
• Most people wait to be introduced and get "this is Tom, he works for me".
cards.theySee: A person who made their introduction easy and then backed it up in the conversation.

signals.t: They invited you to a room above your level
They describe people by one accomplishment, not by job title
People stop talking when they speak
They introduce you vaguely when you have not fed them a line

steps.title: Write your one line
steps.desc: Nine words: what you did, with a number in it.

steps.title: Hand it to them before the room
steps.desc: Send it the day before: "If it comes up, this is the short version."

steps.title: Back it up in one sentence
steps.desc: When someone asks, repeat the same line. Do not upgrade it.

cards.script: (Texted the day before) "If you introduce me tomorrow: 'She cut our onboarding time from 40 days to 9.' That is the useful version."
cards.example: Ines sent her VP one line the night before a client dinner. He used it word for word at the table. Two of the clients asked for her card before dessert, and one hired her team the next quarter.
cards.watchFor: Someone in the room repeats your line back to you later.
cards.ifItFails: They introduce you as "my colleague" and move on. Do not correct them in front of people. Add the line yourself in the next exchange: "I run onboarding — we took it from 40 days to 9." Then send them the line again before the next event, shorter. Do not do this to a boss who needs to be the only story in the room.
cards.counter:
If someone hands you a scripted introduction, they are using your name as currency.
• Notice a pre-written line arriving before an event.
• Say: "I will introduce you, but I will use my own words."
• Vouch only for what you have seen with your own eyes.
cards.insight: Reputation moves at the speed of who repeats it. The trap is a line you cannot back up — the room checks within ten minutes. The harder part is what you say after the introduction lands.

cards.title: Quote Them by Name in Public
cards.remember: Say their idea out loud with their name on it.
cards.when: Your patron said something useful and you are about to present to a wider group.
cards.hook: Credit given in public comes back doubled. And now they have to defend the position you just gave them.
cards.truth:
Public credit does two jobs at once, and only one of them is flattery.
• They hear their name attached to something smart, in front of peers.
• They are now publicly committed to the idea you are pushing.
• The trap is overdoing it. Twice a quarter reads as respect. Weekly reads as sucking up.
cards.theySee: A person who repeats their words accurately and gives them the credit in front of others.

signals.t: They said something sharp in a small meeting
You will present to people senior to you this month
They correct the record when someone misattributes work
You need their public backing for a decision

steps.title: Write down their exact words
steps.desc: Capture the sentence the day they say it, not from memory later.

steps.title: Use it in a bigger room
steps.desc: Say "Ray's framing was" and then quote them, once, accurately.

steps.title: Tell them it landed
steps.desc: Message them after: "Used your line on pricing. The room bought it."

cards.script: "Ray put it best in our review: 'We are not losing on price, we are losing on speed.' That is what this plan fixes."
cards.example: Dan quoted his managing director's exact phrase in a steering committee. The phrase became the project's name. When budget got cut, the MD defended Dan's line item personally, because it carried his own words.
cards.watchFor: They start using your project as an example of their own idea.
cards.ifItFails: They do not react, or a rival claims the idea was theirs first. Do not argue over origin. Put it in writing where it lasts: send the meeting recap naming who said what, once, without complaint. "Recap: Ray's framing on speed, Dana's numbers, my plan. Full doc attached."
cards.counter:
If someone keeps quoting you in public, they are tying you to their plan.
• Notice your own words coming back in rooms you did not attend.
• Say: "That is close. What I actually said was narrower."
• Correct the quote once, early, before it becomes your position.
cards.insight: Praise is cheap and commitment is expensive, and public credit buys both with one sentence. The trap is quoting them on something that later fails — you handed them the blame too. The next question is what you do when their idea is wrong.

cards.title: Take the Blame When Their Bet on You Goes Wrong
cards.principle: Greene: Law 26 — Keep Your Hands Clean, Inverted
cards.remember: Eat the failure in public. Buy their protection forever.
cards.when: A project your patron backed you on fails, and people are looking for someone to blame.
cards.hook: They spent their credit on you. Hand them a clean exit and they will spend it again.
cards.truth:
A patron's real fear is looking stupid for having backed you.
• Say the failure was your call, fast, in front of the same people.
• They keep their standing, and they owe you a large debt.
• The trap is doing this for a failure that was genuinely theirs. That is not loyalty, that is a habit.
cards.theySee: A person who stood up and said "my call" while everyone else looked at the floor.

signals.t: Leadership asks who approved the decision
Your teammates go quiet in the post-mortem
Their name is on the approval email
The failure will not end your career on its own

steps.title: Say it first
steps.desc: Be the first voice in the room: "That was my call and it was wrong."

steps.title: Give the fix in the same breath
steps.desc: Name what you will do differently and by when. No excuses in between.

steps.title: Tell them privately what you did
steps.desc: One line after the meeting: "I took it. You are clear."

cards.script: "That was my call. I pushed the date and I got it wrong. Here is the revised plan and the new date. I will own it either way."
cards.example: When the pilot missed its numbers, Wei said in the review that he had chosen the market and misjudged it. His SVP said nothing. The next quarter the SVP handed Wei a bigger budget and told the room he trusted his judgment.
cards.watchFor: Your patron changes the subject to the fix instead of to the cause.
cards.ifItFails: They let you carry it and never repay — some patrons take the shield and walk. Take the blame once and never again for that person. Say privately: "I took that one. I need you with me on the next one." If the answer is vague, start building a second sponsor. Do not run this move for a failure that could get you fired.
cards.counter:
If someone takes the blame for you fast, they just bought something.
• Notice a junior person absorbing a hit that was not fully theirs.
• Say: "That was a shared call. I signed it."
• Pay it back visibly within a quarter or they will stop protecting you.
cards.insight: Loyalty is proven in the one meeting where it costs you. The tradeoff is real: you carry a visible failure to buy an invisible debt. The harder part is knowing when the debt will never be paid.

cards.title: Send the Result, Not the Check-In
cards.remember: Every quarter, send what happened because of them.
cards.when: Three months have passed since your patron last heard from you.
cards.hook: "Just checking in" is a bill. "Here is what your advice produced" is a dividend.
cards.truth:
Relationships die from empty contact, not from no contact.
• Tie the update to something they gave you: advice, an intro, a decision.
• They get proof that betting on you pays. That feeling is the whole point.
• Most people go quiet for a year and then reappear with an ask. That is transparent.
cards.theySee: A short note showing a number that moved because of something they did.

signals.t: You last spoke more than 90 days ago
Something they advised on actually finished
They no longer reply to your notes within a week
You can state the result as a figure

steps.title: Set a calendar reminder
steps.desc: Four dates a year, one per patron. Do not rely on memory.

steps.title: Write three sentences
steps.desc: What they gave, what you did, what the number was. Nothing else.

steps.title: Close the loop with no ask
steps.desc: End with a period, not a question. Ask nothing this quarter.

cards.script: "You told me to go direct to the customer instead of through the partner. We closed it in 11 days. That is the third one this year. Thank you."
cards.example: Halima sent her old boss one result note every quarter for three years, never asking for anything. When she needed a board reference, he wrote it in an hour and called two people himself.
cards.watchFor: They reply with a new suggestion instead of a thank you.
cards.ifItFails: Two quarterly notes get silence. Change the channel, not the message. Send it as a message another person can pass on, or show up where they are and say it in person in one sentence. "That thing you told me to do worked. Eleven days." In-person results are harder to ignore than email.
cards.counter:
If someone sends you results every quarter, they are keeping an account open.
• Notice regular updates that never contain a request.
• Say: "Good work. Tell me what you want next time."
• Set the terms early or the eventual ask arrives at their chosen moment.
cards.insight: A relationship you only touch when you need it is not a relationship, it is a withdrawal. The trap is sending updates with no result in them — that is a check-in wearing a suit. The next question is what you do the quarter nothing worked.

cards.title: Tell Them What Their Own Team Hides
cards.remember: Tell them what nobody on their team will say.
cards.when: You hear something in the hallway that your patron's direct reports are keeping from them.
cards.hook: Their team tells them what is safe. You tell them what is true, and that makes you irreplaceable.
cards.truth:
Power buys comfort and loses information. They know the trade and hate it.
• Bring one real thing per quarter, never gossip, never names attached to malice.
• They get to act early. That is worth more than any favor you can do.
• The trap is becoming their spy. Report conditions, not people.
cards.theySee: A person who tells them what the room actually thinks, without naming enemies.

signals.t: The meeting version and the hallway version do not match
People say "don't tell him" about something real
They ask you what people are saying
The hidden thing will get more expensive each month

steps.title: Separate fact from gossip
steps.desc: Keep the condition, drop the personalities. "The team does not believe the date" not "Dana said."

steps.title: Say it in person
steps.desc: Never write this one down. Say it face to face or on a call.

steps.title: Offer no verdict
steps.desc: State the thing and stop. Do not recommend who to punish.

cards.script: "Nobody on the floor believes the March date, and they are planning around April. You may already know. I would rather you hear it from me than in the review."
cards.example: Jonas told a VP that her team had quietly built a second plan around a later date. She checked, found it true, and reset the date herself before the board saw it. She started asking Jonas for a read before every big meeting.
cards.watchFor: They ask you a second question instead of defending their team.
cards.ifItFails: They dismiss you or defend the team hard. Drop it immediately and do not repeat it. When the thing breaks — and it will — say one line and nothing more: "This is the March thing." You get one reminder, used quietly, and it buys the next hearing. Do not run this move if the information can be traced to one person who will be fired for it.
cards.counter:
If someone brings you the inside read on your own team, ask what they gain.
• Notice information that always makes the same person look bad.
• Ask: "Who else knows this, and what do you want me to do?"
• Verify it yourself before acting. Informers shape as much as they report.
cards.insight: Every powerful person is starved of one thing they can buy nowhere: the unfiltered read. The tradeoff is that the channel only works while you are seen as clean. The harder part is staying a source without becoming a weapon.

cards.title: Do One Thing For Them You Get No Credit For
cards.principle: Gracián: The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Silent Service
cards.remember: Fix something for them quietly and never mention it.
cards.when: You can prevent a problem for your patron that they will never know existed.
cards.hook: They will find out. They always find out, and it lands harder because you did not tell them.
cards.truth:
Silent help is the one kind that cannot be read as buying favor.
• Kill the problem before it reaches them and say nothing.
• Someone else tells them. Third-party credit is worth triple.
• The trap is hinting. One hint and the whole thing reads as a trade.
cards.theySee: Nothing at the time. Later, someone else tells them what you did.

signals.t: A problem is heading at them and you can stop it
Someone else will see you do it
Fixing it leaves nothing they would notice
News travels in this group within a week

steps.title: Kill the problem
steps.desc: Fix it fully. A half fix that surfaces later looks worse than nothing.

steps.title: Say nothing to them
steps.desc: No email, no hint, no "by the way". Zero mentions.

steps.title: Do not correct the record
steps.desc: If they hear a garbled version, let it stand. Denial sounds like fishing.

cards.script: (To the person who noticed) "Please do not mention it to him. It is handled and it does not need to be a thing."
cards.example: When a client threatened to escalate to Priya's patron, she drove out and fixed it herself and told nobody. The client mentioned it to him two months later at a dinner. He called her that night.
cards.watchFor: They bring it up themselves, weeks later, without you raising it.
cards.ifItFails: Nobody ever tells them. Accept it — that is the price of the move, and complaining costs more than the credit is worth. Run it again with one witness who talks. The version that reaches them from someone else is the only version worth having. Do not use this to hide a mistake you caused.
cards.counter:
If you learn someone quietly saved you, check whether they also arranged the danger.
• Notice a rescue you never asked for from someone with a stake.
• Ask a third party: "How did that problem start?"
• Thank them once. Watch whether the pattern repeats too conveniently.
cards.insight: Help with your name on it is a transaction; help without it is a reputation. The tradeoff is that some of it genuinely vanishes and you get nothing. The next question is how long you can afford to play a game that pays slowly.

cards.title: Read the Signs Before They Fall
cards.principle: Machiavelli: The Prince — The Fortress That Is Already Undermined
cards.remember: Watch their calendar and their allies. Both thin out first.
cards.when: You notice small changes around your patron and you are not sure if they are in trouble.
cards.hook: Nobody announces a fall. The invitations just stop arriving, and then it is too late to plan.
cards.truth:
Power leaks for months before it breaks in public.
• Watch what they get invited to, not what they say.
• Their allies go quiet before their enemies go loud.
• Most proteges find out on the day of the announcement. That is too late to move.
cards.theySee: Nothing from you. They see a person who behaves exactly as before.

signals.t: They stopped being in the meetings they used to run
Someone was hired between them and the top
Two of their supporters took jobs elsewhere in one quarter
Their headcount request got denied this cycle
Their calendar suddenly has space in it

steps.title: Track the invitations
steps.desc: Note which recurring meetings they are still in this month versus last quarter.

steps.title: Count their allies
steps.desc: List who defends them in rooms. If that list shrinks, start planning.

steps.title: Build a second line
steps.desc: Get one real relationship with someone outside their chain this quarter.

cards.script: (To a peer, quietly) "Is Ray still in the Monday operating review? I noticed the notes stopped coming from his side."
cards.example: Yuki saw her patron's name drop off two distribution lists and a new SVP appear above him. She built a working relationship with the new SVP over the next quarter. When her patron was pushed out, she kept her project and her budget.
cards.watchFor: A peer answers your question with a pause and a change of subject.
cards.ifItFails: You cannot tell whether the decline is real. Test it with a small request that only real power can grant: ask them to approve something that needs a signature two levels up. If it stalls for three weeks, the power is already gone. Do not ask them directly whether they are in trouble.
cards.counter:
If your people start quietly building other relationships, they have read your decline.
• Notice reports who suddenly have meetings you did not schedule.
• Say: "Tell me what you are hearing about me."
• Fix the standing or release them cleanly. Holding on makes it faster.
cards.insight: A patron's power is a stock, not a deed, and it trades before the news breaks. The trap is loyalty theater — staying visibly close to a sinking person costs you with the winners. The harder part is doing this without becoming the person everyone saw leave first.

cards.title: Defend Them Once in Public, Then Go Quiet
cards.principle: Greene: Law 36 — Disdain Things You Cannot Have
cards.remember: Say one loyal thing out loud. Then stop talking about it.
cards.when: Your patron has lost their position and people are talking about them in front of you.
cards.hook: Say nothing and you are a rat. Say it ten times and you go down with them. Say it once.
cards.truth:
One public defense is loyalty. Repeated defense is a faction, and factions lose together.
• Say one clean, factual thing in front of witnesses.
• People remember that you did not join the pile-on.
• The trap is arguing the case. Nobody is relitigating it, they are picking sides.
cards.theySee: A person who said one respectful thing and then let the subject drop.

signals.t: People criticize them openly who never did before
Someone asks you directly what you thought of them
The incoming leader is in the room during the talk
Their former supporters say nothing at all

steps.title: Prepare one sentence
steps.desc: Write a factual line about what they did well. One fact, no opinion.

steps.title: Say it once, in a room
steps.desc: Deliver it when the criticism starts, then change the subject yourself.

steps.title: Never bring it up again
steps.desc: If someone reopens it, say "I said my piece" and move on.

cards.script: "He hired half the people in this room, including me. That is what I know. Anyway — where are we on the March date?"
cards.example: When the group director was fired, the room turned on him. Elena said he had built the team that was still running and then moved to the next agenda item. The new director told her privately that she was the only one he would trust with bad news.
cards.watchFor: The room drops the subject when you change it.
cards.ifItFails: Someone pushes back and demands you justify the defense. Do not argue the record. Hand it back: "You may be right. I only know what he did for me." Then stop speaking. Do not defend a patron who was removed for something the new leadership calls a red line — that loyalty gets read as complicity.
cards.counter:
If someone defends a fallen leader once and stops, they are managing their record, not grieving.
• Notice a single loyal line followed by a topic change.
• Say nothing about it. Note who spoke and who piled on.
• The ones who piled on will do it to you next time.
cards.insight: Loyalty is priced by the new leadership, and they are watching exactly one thing: whether you can be trusted when it costs you. The tradeoff is that one sentence buys respect and two buys suspicion. The move that follows is what you do with their contacts.

cards.title: Keep Their Network After They Lose Their Title
cards.principle: Granovetter: The Strength of Weak Ties
cards.remember: Their contacts stay valuable after their job disappears.
cards.when: Your patron has left, been pushed out, or retired, and their circle is still intact.
cards.hook: They lost the title. They did not lose the twenty people who take their call.
cards.truth:
A fallen patron is worth more than people think and costs almost nothing to keep.
• Their relationships outlive their job by years.
• Nobody calls them now. Your call lands with full weight.
• The trap is calling only when you want a name. Call before you need one.
cards.theySee: A person who kept calling after the title went away, when almost nobody else did.

signals.t: They mention nobody calls anymore
Their old contacts still reply to them
They are talking to boards or other firms
They have hours they did not have before

steps.title: Call within two weeks
steps.desc: Not email. Call, and do not ask for anything on that call.

steps.title: Ask what they are doing next
steps.desc: Let them talk about the next thing. Offer to help with one piece of it.

steps.title: Ask for one introduction later
steps.desc: Wait a full quarter. Then ask for one name, not a list.

cards.script: (On the call) "No agenda. I wanted to hear what you are doing next and whether I can be useful on any of it."
cards.example: When his managing director was forced out, Aziz called him the same week with no ask. He helped with two hiring calls over the next year. When the MD landed at a bigger firm, Aziz was his second hire.
cards.watchFor: They start telling you about the next job before you ask about it.
cards.ifItFails: They are bitter and the call goes badly. Do not push and do not counsel them. Send one short note two months later tied to something real: "Saw the Acme announcement. Congratulations — call me if you need hands." Fallen people re-emerge on their own schedule; your job is to still be reachable when they do.
cards.counter:
If someone stays close after you lose your seat, they are holding an option on your comeback.
• Notice who calls in the first two weeks after the fall.
• Say: "Thanks for calling. I will remember who did."
• Mean it. That list is the foundation of the next thing you build.
cards.insight: Titles expire and relationships do not, which is why the cheapest network in the world is the one everyone else just dropped. The tradeoff is time spent on someone who may never rise again. The next question is whether you are building patrons or becoming one.
